claims.text: The studied material is a powder-metallurgy-produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy contains dual BCC phases and a minor sigma phase.
Selective oxidation of Al and Ti governs the high-temperature oxidation resistance of the HEA.
The multiphase BCC/sigma microstructure provides efficient localized grain-boundary diffusion paths.
Preferential oxidation of Al and Ti produces a spinel oxide.
Above a critical temperature of approximately 800 °C, the multiphase microstructure enhances oxygen diffusion and selective oxidation.
Selective oxidation forms a coherent spinel scale that adheres to the substrate.
The coherent spinel scale protects the underlying HEA from further oxidation.
Samples exposed above 800 °C will develop a distinct spinel-structured oxide layer detectable by XRD and microscopy.
High-temperature samples will exhibit lower oxidation rates than samples treated at lower temperatures or containing less Al and Ti.
AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 has greater wear resistance at 800–900 °C than at lower test temperatures.
Lower-temperature exposure or reduction of spinel-forming elements will prevent formation of a coherent protective oxide layer.
Lower-temperature samples will have lower wear resistance than samples tested at 800–900 °C.
Reducing Al and Ti concentrations will result in lower wear resistance.
The proposed mechanism applies in oxidizing atmospheres above approximately 800 °C but may not apply in inert atmospheres or below that temperature.
Comparing the standard alloy with an Al/Ti-reduced variant under otherwise identical oxidation treatments can test the proposed role of Al and Ti.
A lack of a significant difference in spinel-scale formation, oxidation behavior, and wear resistance between the standard and Al/Ti-reduced alloys would falsify the hypothesis.
The contribution of the sigma phase, grain-boundary chemistry, and processing history to scale formation and adherence remains uncertain.
